transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-09-14 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~62m
- Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Anil (Redwood SA), David (Hemlock CISO), Sara (Platform), Priyanka (Legal), Omar (DevOps)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Hemlock is evaluating Redwood for customer-facing inference. Primary concerns: where logs live, ability to run in-region (EU/US) for GDPR/sectoral rules, keystore residency and escrow, ability to run private control plane or Dedicated GPUs, and how to produce audit evidence for legal hold and e-discovery. They want short-term pilot to validate log redaction and latency.

Topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs; keystore/KMS residency; log retention and redaction; SOC2/HIPAA evidence; region locking and fallback routing; SLA and canary rollouts.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll kick off, quick intros. I'm Lena, AE on the Redwood inference team. Marco's our systems engineer, Anil helps on architecture.
[00:18] David: Hi, David here, CISO at Hemlock, and Sara my platform lead, Priyanka from legal, Omar from DevOps.
[00:32] Marco: Great thanks. Quick agenda: understand current stack, residency constraints, logging/evidence needs, and then talk options (hosted, dedicated, private).
[00:48] Omar: To level-set, we run most systems in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Some regulated workloads must never leave eu data centers, and legal hold means we may need to freeze evidence for up to 7 years.
[01:05] Priyanka: also HIPAA-ish concerns for small subset of customers, plus PCI-lite controls on transaction metadata, so we need keystore-level separation and strong audit trail.
[01:22] Marco: Understood. High level, Redwood Hosted can do region-scoped hosting but we do retain some control-plane telemetry; Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools and network isolation, and Private gives you customer-controlled control plane + on-prem options.
[01:38] David: Do you have SOC 2 Type II plus HIPAA attestation artifacts? We need to see evidence and some sample audit logs.
[01:48] Lena: Yes we have SOC2 Type II and a HIPAA compliance pack. I'll share the packet after this call — redacted artifacts and a short notes deck. (link will be in follow-up).
[02:06] Sara: For evidence, our auditors ask for immutable trails and proof of key handling. If keys are in a Redwood-managed KMS in another country that could be a showstopper.
[02:20] Marco: Right, so we support customer-managed KMS integrations (bring-your-own-key), and for Dedicated/Private we can route keys to your HSM/KMS. There's also a local keystore option where the control plane never sees raw keys.
[02:40] Priyanka: local keystore meaning? Is that on-prem or in VPC? We need to document who has access and where it lives.
[02:52] Anil: The local keystore option places key material under customer control in their VPC or HSM, while Redwood holds only a reference. That reduces control plane exposure and simplifies residency evidence.
[03:10] Omar: On logs — can we turn off full request/response logging? We need to avoid storing PII. Our legal wants only token-level metadata and sanitized prompts in most cases.
[03:24] Marco: We have several modes: full, minimal (only token counts, latency), and redacted (rules-based redaction before storage). Redaction is best-effort at the moment — there's still edge cases — we can show sample output.
[03:38] David: If redaction misses something, who owns the record? We need SLA on redaction effectiveness or ability to purge.
[03:48] Lena: We can implement retention windows and on-demand purging for Dedicated/Private. Hosted has a standard retention policy but enterprise customers can negotiate longer or shorter windows and sanitized views.
[04:02] Priyanka: We need legal hold capability: when litigation hits we must be able to lock down artifacts and provide certified exports. Does Redwood provide a certified export for audit?
[04:14] Marco: We provide export bundles with checksums and chain-of custody metadata for Dedicated/Private. For Hosted we can produce logs and metadata but chain-of-custody is more limited; we can work on an attested export with additional contracts.
[04:34] Sara: Another one — region-locking and fallback. We want EU traffic to stay in EU — but if capacity is constrained do you fallback to US? That breaks GDPR for certain data classes.
[04:46] Anil: We support strict region-locking policies: you can declare a route that only uses eu-west instances. We also support fallback policies but they are opt-in; for regulated profiles you can disable fallback entirely and fail rather than cross-border.
[05:00] David: Good. Cost/latency tradeoff question — Dedicated GPUs lower cross-request latency; if we keep everything in region will that spike cost significantly?
[05:12] Marco: Somewhat. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and you avoid cross-region egress; Hosted can be cheaper at low throughput. We can model a cost baseline once we get your qps and typical token lengths.
[05:30] Omar: On encryption and escrow — do you support split-key escrow or dual control for legal access? We need two-person access for release.
[05:40] Marco: We can integrate with customer HSMs and support multi-party approval workflows for key-escrow, though the workflow is typically part of Private engagements. We'll need to scope the process.
[05:58] Priyanka: Who at Redwood would sign an SOC addendum or data processing addendum? We need contractual language for DPA and subprocessors.
[06:10] Lena: Legal will handle the DPA; I'll loop in our contracts team. We can provide standard DPA and discuss subprocessors; we try to be transparent on subprocessors for Hosted.
[06:28] David: Can you walk us through an example evidence path for a single user transaction — from request to potential e-discovery export?
[06:40] Marco: Sure. Flow: client -> Redwood API endpoint in region -> request is routed to model shard -> optional KV cache lookup -> inference returns -> response streamed to client. Logs are emitted at each stage: request metadata, routing decision, model id, token counts. If redaction enabled the raw prompt is replaced before persistent storage. For Dedicated/Private you can retain logs in your S3 and we produce a signed export with checksums.
[07:12] Sara: What about ephemeral KV cache? If KV cache used for context, is that stored persistently and does it persist across restarts?
[07:22] Marco: KV cache is normally in-memory and ephemeral; for performance we persist small checkpoints but we can disable persistence for regulated workloads so nothing is written to disk. There's also an encrypted checkpoint option.
[07:40] Omar: Any limitation on encryption algorithms? FIPS? We need FIPS-validated crypto for some controls.
[07:48] Anil: We can integrate with FIPS-validated HSMs and support FIPS TLS stacks for Dedicated/Private. Hosted may have limitations depending on region/hypervisor. We'll capture specifics for you.
[08:06] David: Now about HIPAA — for that subset, do you recommend Hosted or Dedicated?
[08:14] Marco: Usually we advise Dedicated or Private for PHI because of stronger tenant isolation and the ability to run in a fully customer-managed network; Hosted can be made HIPAA-compatible with BAAs and configuration but Dedicated reduces operational risk.
[08:32] Priyanka: BAAs — do you sign BAAs for Hosted?
[08:36] Lena: We do sign BAAs with enterprise customers under specific contractual terms. We'll share the template.
[08:44] David: Regarding monitoring — our SOC team wants SIEM integration and not just exported CSVs. Integrations with Splunk or Datadog are needed.
[08:52] Marco: We support log forwarding to customer SIEMs for Dedicated/Private; Hosted can forward structured telemetry but certain raw artifacts won't be exported. We'll enumerate available streams.
[09:08] Omar: How do you handle multi-tenant metadata? We need tenant isolation and clear separation on index/keying so one tenant's prompts can't be accessed by another.
[09:18] Anil: Tenant isolation is enforced at routing and storage layers. Dedicated provides physical pool separation; Hosted is logically multitenant with strong isolation boundaries. We'll include architecture diagrams.
[09:34] Priyanka: For e-discovery export we also need redaction logs showing what was removed and why. Can Redwood produce a redaction audit trail?
[09:46] Marco: We can produce a redaction audit that shows original snippet reference (hash), applied rule, and resulting redacted text; it's part of the export bundle for Dedicated/Private.
[10:00] David: Ok great. Next, performance: we may want to run a bench where we send realistic payloads. Can you support benchmarking in our EU region?
[10:12] Marco: Yes, we can spin up a dedicated trial in eu-west and run a small benchmark with your sample prompts. We'll need creds and sample load.
[10:24] Lena: I'll put together a checklist of what we need from Hemlock to run the pilot.
[10:32] Priyanka: For evidence packages, please obfuscate any Redwood internal IPs when you share—legal needs redacted docs.
[10:44] Lena: understood. We'll redact internal infra details.
[10:50] David: On fallback routing — if a region is down, how do you prove we didn't route EU PII to US? We need deterministic logging for routing decisions.
[10:58] Marco: Routing decisions are logged with timestamps and region tags. For strict policies we will fail rather than reroute; logs will show the failure and reason.
[11:12] Omar: There's also a need for per-request consent flags — to mark certain requests as non-persisted or ephemeral. Is that supported?
[11:22] Marco: Yes, we have request-level flags for no-persist and no-logs. They can be honored at runtime; however, certain metrics (like billing token counts) still exist in aggregate. We'll show how that looks.
[11:36] Sara: Any limitations on streaming output with no-persist? We rely on streaming for UX.
[11:44] Marco: Streaming is supported; no-persist prevents persistent storage but may still use transient buffers. We'll document exactly what touches disk.
[11:58] David: Good. Can you outline the rough timeline and decision gating Hemlock should expect? We likely need: 1) legal review of DPA and BAA, 2) pilot, 3) security assessment, 4) go/no-go.
[12:12] Lena: That's accurate. Typical pilot is 4–6 weeks. Security assessment timelines depend on Hemlock's internal SOC schedule.
[12:24] Priyanka: One more: we require that only named Redwood engineers can access audit bundles and that access is logged. Is that doable?
[12:36] Anil: We can create a scoped access role and log everything. For Private it's straightforward; for Dedicated we'll implement a role-based ACL and show the audit trails.
[12:50] Marco: Quick note: sometimes transcription of our documentation uses 'KV cash' or 'V-P-C' in automated exports — apologies for that, you'll see similar artifacts in the auto notes.
[13:05] Lena: Alright, let's recap next steps. Marco will size a Dedicated pilot in eu-west. I'll send SOC2/HIPAA package and contract contacts. Hemlock to provide retention matrix and sample prompts for benchmarking. We'll aim to reconvene week of 2027-09-22.
[13:28] David: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[13:32] (call wraps; informal chat continues for a few minutes about calendaring)

Notes on quality: transcript contains a few auto-generated mis-hearings, proper names may be slightly off; timestamps are periodic. Shared artifacts referenced: security-deck.pdf (link), pilot-checklist.xlsx (link).

End of transcript.
